extracted.intended_audience: authors (especially fiction writers) and self-publishing/indie authors seeking guidance on line editing or whether to hire a line editor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what line editing is, how it differs from copy editing, what specific improvements a line edit makes to a manuscript, and practical self-editing do's and don'ts for book-length fiction or prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line editing (scope and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A line editor works through a manuscript, line-by-line, with a laser-sharp focus on the stylistic and structural aspects of the writing. It’s much more than a simple proof — a well-done line edit will bring clarity, precision, and impact to your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence-level focus: suggestions for word choice, syntax, and tone to enhance the author’s voice and the text’s overall effectiveness. Line editing is more in-depth and subjective than copy editing and may include interpretive changes to improve clarity and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy editing (mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editing is a general term for editing a piece of text, encompassing mechanics like spelling, grammar, and punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editing is fairly cut-and-dried compared with line editing; it addresses mechanical correctness (spelling, grammar, punctuation, consistency) rather than stylistic choices or voice. Example edits: delete superfluous phrases, fix commas, split sentences for clarity when strictly mechanical issues demand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthens the prose with better word choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Line editing facilitates strong, precise word choice and gets rid of clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A line editor will note where word choice can be improved and suggest alternatives (avoid clichés like “star-crossed lovers” or “the whole world was against them”); replace weak, vague wording (e.g., “It made Clothilde feel bad”) with specific description; favour showing over telling; question awkward or unclear diction (e.g., is “meaty fragrance” the intended image?). Avoid thesaurus overuse (see don'ts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trims the fat for a tighter reading experience (concision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Line editing ensures that syntax is concise, cutting sentences and even whole passages when necessary to improve readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delete superfluous phrases, split long unwieldy sentences, remove unnecessary repetition (don’t restate the same fact twice in different words), and condense phrasing so readers can navigate sentences more easily. Example: break a very long sentence into two and remove redundant mentions of a plot point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fills in gaps that could confuse the reader (consistency & clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A line edit will fix plot and character inconsistencies and simple descriptive blunders that could confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out and correct things like contradictory character reactions (e.g., a vampire gagging at blood without explanation), missing motivations, or descriptive slips; either clarify the reason or change the reaction/description to be consistent with established facts. This can include flagging missing events or chronology issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improves the flow by correcting mood and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A line edit corrects writing that strikes the wrong tone and adjusts mood to suit the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tone matches the intended emotional register (e.g., climactic scenes should feel grave, not silly); choose stronger, appropriate verbs; remove incongruous similes or anachronisms (e.g., a historical character referencing a modern object); eliminate descriptors that undermine the scene’s gravity (e.g., incongruous physical detail at a death scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Builds on prose to improve reader’s overall understanding (interpretive enhancement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Line edits can do more than correct: they can add a new layer of meaning and reveal subtext to improve a reader’s understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical fixes, a line editor may rephrase or highlight details that deepen characterization or clarify implicit attitudes (example: a line edit that reveals Jane’s dislike of walking). This is an interpretive, subjective part of line editing intended to strengthen narrative impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-editing tip: Set your manuscript aside
rubrics_metrics.description: Set your manuscript aside for a few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let your own language become new to you again so you can approach it with some distance and more effectively spot problems and opportunities for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-editing tip: Read everything out loud
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listening to the prose helps you judge sentence flow, order, naturalness of speech, and physical 'breath' in sentences; if you gasp for breath before a sentence ends or stumble on a word, revise for clarity or rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-editing tip: Audit for your own personal clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Audit for your own personal clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond stock clichés (e.g., 'raining cats and dogs'), watch for repeated personal tics—overuse of certain punctuation (semicolons), favorite verbs or adverbs, or recurring character mannerisms—and revise to avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't: Become a thesaurus junkie
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to improving your word choice, a thesaurus can definitely help. But going overboard with it will ruin your prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting simple, appropriate words with overwrought synonyms that distract the reader (example: turning 'blue eyes' into 'ultramarine orbs'). Use the best word, not the most ornate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't: Insult your reader / spoon-feed
rubrics_metrics.description: When editing for clarity, don’t go too far and start spoon-feeding your readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust readers’ intelligence—guide rather than over-explain. Avoid excessive exposition or explanatory asides that treat the reader as incapable of inferring subtext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't: Refuse to ask for help
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you decide not to hire a professional editor, that doesn't mean you must go it alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider second readers, critique circles, or hiring a professional editor for outside perspective; refusing feedback can leave problems in the manuscript that you can’t see yourself.
